query: Consider the following context: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for next-generation nuclear applications, particularly fusion reactors, due to their excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In that context, which material can be used for low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten-based high-entropy alloy containing vanadium, chromium, and other low-activation elements can serve as a promising low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-dominant refractory HEA ingot (e.g., W–V–Cr–X) prepared by arc or vacuum induction melting in as-cast form.
generation.intervention: Homogenize the alloy and subject it to neutron/ion irradiation testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature service (≥800 °C) under representative fusion reactor conditions of thermal loads, helium implantation, and neutron fluence.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined grain boundaries stabilized by multi-element high-entropy effects and low-activation solute additions.
generation.mechanism: The multiple principal elements reduce defect mobility and mitigate irradiation damage, while limiting radioactive isotopes formed, thus improving radiation tolerance and reducing activation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced high-temperature mechanical performance and reduced long-lived radioactivation compared to conventional tungsten-based alloys.
generation.baseline: Pure tungsten or standard tungsten alloys that exhibit higher Swiss-cheese-like damage from helium bubbles and increased long-term activation.
generation.boundary: Alloy composition must balance high-entropy effects with solute diffusivity; long-duration irradiation testing is needed to confirm minimal activation and stable microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: Long-term void swelling, helium- and hydrogen-induced damage, and mechanical stability under high fluence require further empirical validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare an as-cast W–V–Cr–X high-entropy alloy with pure W and other established PFC materials under identical high-flux neutron/ion irradiation conditions at ≥800 °C for extended durations.
measurements: Radiation-induced swelling and microstructure evolution (TEM, SEM)
Helium bubble density and size distribution (TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy shows no improved tolerance to damage or reduction in activation compared to conventional W-based alloys, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Clean energy production is the cornerstone of our time. Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] .
